title: The Educated Barbarian: Hagakure analysis (part. 17)
summary: In part 17 of his Hagakure reading series, NH discusses passages on pride and service, perfectionism (killing the ox by fixing its horns), moderation, internal versus external willpower, and how to give advice. He stresses kindness, never shaming people, since attacked beliefs only harden, and letting people believe an idea came from them.
claims: Acts of service are the things you do willingly without being paid; the people you serve this way are the ones who truly matter to you
Pride that puts you above service ends up limiting you, because passing down knowledge and being helpful keeps society together and advancing
Pride in exceptional qualities is justified, but without kindness the other qualities lose their shine
Seeing yourself as perfect stops you working; staying open to others' criticism keeps you improving
Much morality is self-preservation: behaving morally keeps you in good standing within society, which benefits you
Chasing a tiny perfection can ruin something that was fine, like killing the ox by straightening its horns
Nothing is good in excess, including training: training too much leaves you overtrained and unable to progress
Some things can be harmful even in small quantities, so 'the dose makes the poison' only cuts one way
Internal willpower is unseen discipline, like training when you do not want to or skipping bad food; external willpower is shown to others, like standing your ground
Only internal willpower makes you a doormat; only external makes you a tyrant; a balance is needed
People who loudly display willpower, like announcing a diet to 50 people, often lack internal willpower
Unused willpower rusts; you must practice it
Ego often keeps people from the easy way out of a confrontation; there is always a face-saving solution
Public reproaches come from the ego of the person making them, who often projects their own faults onto you
People only take fitness advice from someone who visibly embodies what they preach; if you are not big, people will not listen
We see others' mistakes far more easily than our own, so keep a circle of people around you
Telling someone they are stupid makes them cling to their behavior as part of their identity
NH cites a study that people attacked for believing misinformation become more attached to it
Manipulators install prepared responses in their followers so counterarguments trigger rehearsed rebuttals
People only change if they think the idea came from them, as in Inception
Praising improvement works for most people, but some, praised too much or too little growing up, relapse when praised and double down when criticized
